Failure to comply with expectaƟons regarding academic integrity will result in serious penalƟes that will have repercussions for the rest of your academic career. policies.name: AI Usage
description: However, in an educational environment you should get used to using AI as a tutor rather than an assistant. Use it to help you do the work, don't offload the work to it. Learn from the explanations provided, then apply that understanding to your work. Repeat this process as needed. AI assistants have infinite patience for your questions.

When you graduate, you will be competing with people who learned to code before AI assistants existed. These people may use AI for their daily work today, but they benefit from having built their foundational knowledge without relying on it during their formative years. This likely makes them better equipped and more resilient to handle the inherent uncertainty in building software systems

When you enter the tech-related workforce, employers will expect you to solve coding problems independently without the use of AI tools. For sure, this will include during job interviews but it also includes brainstorming with teammates. You must be able to think creativelyand communicate about your code without relying on AI. Even if you excel at programming with AI assistance, being unable to demonstrate your skills without it will significantly hinder your job prospects.

beats.label: Overview
beats.text:
Overview

In this unit, we will:

  1. Discuss what an algorithm is.
  2. Look at two ways to represent them:
    1. Pseudocode
    2. Flow diagrams
  3. Look at an important historical development in computer science regarding algorithms: The Turing Machine

beats.label: Definition?
beats.text:
Definition?

Definition (Intuitive): An algorithm is a set of instructions that is designed to accomplish a task.

This is not very formal (and so hard to do much with), so people have tried to take more formal and mathematical approaches. Among them, there have been three notable perspectives:

  • Lambda Calculus (Alonzo Church). An algorithm is a series of applications of mathematical functions and transformations.
  • Recursive Functions (Kurt Godel, Stephen Kleene). An algorithm is a set of simple mathematical functions that can be built into increasingly complex functions through repetition.
  • Turing Machines (Alan Turing). An algorithm is a set of rules for a hypothetical machine that reads and writes symbols on an infinite tape.

All of these approaches are independent and equivalent ways of defining algorithms and computability. We will look at how a Turing Machine works later.

beats.label: Pseudocode
beats.text:
Pseudocode

Suppose you are nuclear engineer who is tasked with maintaining a certain part of a nuclear reactor. You notice that the part you are supposed to watch is acting unusually. You know you need to add a particular type of coolant, but can't remember which one or how much and if you are off by even a little bit, the part could fail and the entire facility could explode. You ask your supervisor and their response is: 'Just add a little of the blue stuff.'

How helpful was your supervisor's direction?

Pseudocode is a way of trying to make an algorithm explicit enough that there is no ambiguity as to what should be done, but not so explicit that it becomes difficult to parse, requiring more mental energy and time than the process is worth.

No universal convention. Large range in degree of formality. One example below.

Input: a collection A of numbers a1, a2, a3, ..., an
Outpt: a number ai from the collection such that aj is less than or equal to ai for all j=1,2,...,n

FIND-MAXIMUM(A)
1  max <-- A[1]
2  FOR i from 2 to A.length
3      IF A[i] > max THEN
4          max <-- A[i]
5      END IF
6  END FOR
7  RETURN  max

beats.label: Pseudocode:
beats.text:
Pseudocode: Examples

Here is the same task (addition of two numbers), but approached in three very different ways.


Version: Accumulation
Input: a,b
Output: sum of a and b

ADD(a,b)
1  sum <-- 0
2  sum <-- sum + a>
3  sum <-- sum + b>
4  RETURN sum

Version: Iteration
Input: a,b
Output: sum of a and b

ADD(a,b)
1  sum <-- a
2  REPEAT b times
3      sum <-- sum + 1
4  END REPEAT
5  RETURN sum
Version: Recursion
Input: a,b
Output: sum of a and b

ADD(a,b)
1  IF b == 0 THEN
2      RETURN a
3  END IF
4  RETURN Add(a+1, b-1)

beats.label: Visual
beats.text:
Visual representation of algorithms

Above is a visual version of the Add algorithm below:
Input: a,b
Output: sum of a and b

ADD(a,b)
1  sum <-- a
2  REPEAT b times
3      sum <-- sum + 1
4  END REPEAT
5  RETURN sum

beats.label: Tedium
beats.text:
Tedium

Try carrying out the steps of the algorithm below very carefully and methodically.

Input: sequence A = {a1, a2, ..., aN} of integersOutput: a reordering B = {b1, b2, ..., bN} of a1, a2, ..., aN such that bi <= bj whenever i<= j
InsertionSort(A)
1  FOR j from 2 to n
2      key <-- A[j]
3      i <-- j-1
4      WHILE i > 0 and A[i] > key
5          A[i+1] <-- A[i]
6          i <--i-1
7      END WHILE
8      A[i+1] <-- key
9  END FOR
10 RETURN A

As we start to formalize algorithms, carrying them out becomes quite tedious. If only we had a happy little helper who would gladly punch away at these highly precise, yet highly monotonous microtasks. If only...

But first we should maybe ask outselves whether having such a helper would even be useful. In particular, could we even reasonably guarantee that it would be competent? That is, that it would be able to solve any algorithm that we threw at it?

To that end, we now turn to the Turing machine.

beats.label: Turing
beats.text:
Turing machine components

There are three core components of Turing machine:

  1. Infinite tape
  2. Tape head
  3. Transition table

beats.label: What
beats.text: What does a Turing machine do?

beats.label: Transition
beats.text: Transition table

beats.label: Turing
beats.text:
Turing Machine: Even or Odd Task: Setup

Tape alphabet: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7,9,e,o

Task: Check if a number is even or odd.

The tape alphabet and task are fixed. It is up to us to determine:

  1. How many states the tape head can take (keeping in mind that there is always a START and HALT state)
  2. The transition table for those states

beats.label: Transition
beats.text:
Transition diagram

It can be very easy for a human mind to lose sight of what path of states and choices a Turing machine is making. A transition diagram helps make that more clear. Above we show the transition diagram for one Turing machine configuration that successfully completes the even or odd task mentioned previously.

beats.label: Unwieldy
beats.text:
Unwieldy

Turing Machines become unwiedly quite fast. The image above is of a transition diagram for a turing machine that accomplishes the task of 'subtraction.' Note how complex that already is.

beats.label: Why
beats.text:
Why do we care about Turing machines?

The three main approaches of formalism (Church's Lambda Calculus, Godel's Recursive Functions, and Turing's Turing machines') are all equivalent. Each approach has at least one instance where its perspective is uniquely helpful. Thinking about algorithmic formalism through the Turing machine perspective is especially helpful when looking at hardware (which we will do in the next unit).

Church-Turing thesis: Our intuitive notion of an algorithm is perfectly captured by the formal mathematical concept of a Turing machine.

The Church-Turing thesis is unproven (and unprovable), but most computer scientists believe it. From this came the notion of Turing Completeness for programming languages, whereby if a language can simulate a Turing machine, it can perform any computation that any other computer can (and by the Church-Turing thesis, can carry out any algorithm that a human could).
